CLASS 33 · AGES 4–5 · 29 HELPER LESSONS

Community Helpers & Our Neighborhood.

HOW THIS CLASS WORKS

Meet the people who keep our neighborhood running.

Every helper in this class has its own step-by-step lesson: look at the picture together, learn what the job really is, say the parent script, ask the questions, play the practice game and finish with a small understanding check. One helper a day is plenty — the whole class is a month of five-minute sessions, in whatever order your child’s curiosity points.

Start with the helpers your child already meets — doctor, bus driver, teacher — then follow the given order for the full journey: health helpers, safety helpers, learning helpers, food and growing helpers, and the people who build and fix everything else.

HELPERS AND THEIR RULES

The people who help, the rules that call them.

Class 33 names the helpers — firefighters, police officers, the crossing guard; Class 39 · Staying Safe rehearses the moments that bring them: the helping shelf — Safety Hero’s stop-ask-tell, ask-for-help, if-you’re-lost, stay-with-your-group and tell-if-you’re-hurt — plus fire safety’s calm three moves. Helpers here, the asking-for-help words next door.

WORDS FOR EVERY WALK

Class 44 · Position & Direction Words.

Class 33 walks the neighborhood — the doctor, the mailbox, the fire station — and every single walk runs on direction words: toward the corner, across the street, next to the park, away from home. The Prepositions for kids class prints those walking words as cards: twenty-two position and direction flashcards for ages 4–5, all on the one class page, each with a way to act it out before the next walk.

HELPERS LIVE NEXT DOOR TOO

Class 45 · Family & Friends.

Class 33 walks the big neighborhood — the doctor, the mailbox, the fire station — and the Family & Friends class walks the small one: the house and the street around it. Mum, dad, grandma, the neighbor who waves every morning, the teacher waiting at the door — thirty-five printable family member flashcards for ages 4–5, all on the one page, each with one way to be a helper at home today.

COMMUNITY HELPERS WORKSHEET ACTIVITY · CLASS 33 · AGES 4–5

Doctor — solve it right on the sheet.

Trace DOCTOR, match the doctor to the stethoscope, bandage and thermometer, circle the healthy habits, count the medicine bottles and draw one way you care for your body.

THE WORKSHEET — WRITE AND DRAW RIGHT ON IT

Your sheet is ready.

Pick a color or the eraser, then trace, match, circle, count and draw straight on the sheet with your finger, a stylus or the mouse. Press Save my work when you are proud — that is what marks this activity cleared for your child.

Solving on the sheet needs JavaScript. The printable twin at /worksheets/community-helpers-and-our-neighborhooddoctor/ / always works.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: What a doctor’s tools are for, which everyday habits keep bodies healthy, and how to read and write the word DOCTOR.

Knowledge to have ready: Your child needs a little vocabulary first: a doctor helps sick and hurt people, a stethoscope listens to heartbeats, a bandage protects a healing cut, and a thermometer checks temperature. Say each tool’s name before the pencil starts.

Why this activity matters: Doctors become familiar instead of frightening when children meet their tools on paper first. The healthy-habit grid also turns the worksheet into a gentle health talk, and the tracing row builds the same pre-writing muscles the alphabet class uses.

  • Community helper vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Healthy-habit awareness
  • Counting to 5
  • Word tracing
  • Drawing from life

What to say before you start: "This is a doctor — his tools help him take care of people. Trace his name, then find the three tools that belong with him. Now look at the six pictures: which ones show something healthy? Count the bottles slowly with your finger, and finish by drawing how YOU keep your body strong."

What to look for on the sheet: Point at the big picture together: the doctor wears a white coat and a blue tie and a stethoscope around his neck. In the match row, ask which tool would listen to a heartbeat. In the grid, ask your child to explain WHY a picture is or is not a healthy habit.

Questions to ask along the way: "Which doctor’s tool listens to your heart?" "Why do we wash hands before seeing the doctor?" "Which of the six habits do you do every day?" "What number did the medicine bottles count up to?"

Helpful hints without giving it away: If a match line is hard, name the tools first and ask what each one touches. In the circle row, the tricky tiles are the ones that look fun — ask "does this help your body or just feel fun right now?" Count the bottles with one touch per bottle so the count stays honest.

Parent tips: Keep doctor talk friendly and honest — doctors help, and saying how you feel to a doctor is always allowed. Let your child own the pencil: the tracing can be wobbly and the drawing messy; the thinking is the work.

Understanding check: Ask: "Which tool listens to the heart? Name one healthy habit from the grid. How many bottles?" Right tool, one habit, the right count = the sheet landed.

Real-life practice: Walk the healthy-habit grid at home today: the apple at snack time, the teeth brushing tonight, the running in the yard. Real repetition is what turns a circled picture into a habit.

Firefighter — solve it right on the sheet.

Trace FIRE FIGHTER, match the firefighter to the hose, helmet and fire truck, circle the tools a firefighter uses, count the fire helmets and draw stop-drop-and-roll.

THE WORKSHEET — WRITE AND DRAW RIGHT ON IT

Your sheet is ready.

Pick a color or the eraser, then trace, match, circle, count and draw straight on the sheet with your finger, a stylus or the mouse. Press Save my work when you are proud — that is what marks this activity cleared for your child.

Solving on the sheet needs JavaScript. The printable twin at /worksheets/community-helpers-and-our-neighborhoodfirefighter/ / always works.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: What a firefighter wears and carries, which tools fight fires, and the emergency move every child should own: stop, drop and roll.

Knowledge to have ready: Before starting, name the gear together: the helmet protects the head, the hose carries water, the truck rushes everything to the fire. Explain stop-drop-and-roll in one sentence — if clothes ever catch fire, we stop, drop to the ground, and roll until the fire is out.

Why this activity matters: Fire safety is a skill with real stakes, and rehearsal is what makes it stick. The tool grid sharpens "who uses what" thinking, the helmet count is gentle number practice, and the draw box lets your child rehearse the emergency move with their own hands.

  • Emergency vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Stop-drop-and-roll rehearsal
  • Counting to 7
  • Word tracing
  • Safety drawing

What to say before you start: "This is a firefighter. Trace the two words, then connect him to his hose, his helmet and his truck. Now look at the six tools — a firefighter carries some of them, but a couple belong to a mechanic or a student. Count the helmets with your finger, and then draw the safety move: stop, drop, and roll."

What to look for on the sheet: Find the yellow stripes on the firefighter’s coat and the badge on the helmet — real gear details to spot. In the grid, ask which tool sprays water and which one would fix a car instead. In the count row, helmets point in different directions; touch each one so none is counted twice.

Questions to ask along the way: "What does the hose carry?" "Why does a firefighter wear a helmet?" "Which two tools in the grid are NOT for fighting fires?" "Show me stop, drop, and roll — can you do it on the carpet?"

Helpful hints without giving it away: If the grid stalls, sort out loud: "sprays water, chops, lights the dark, puts out small fires — what’s left?" For the count, group the helmets into the top row and the bottom row first, then add the groups.

Parent tips: Practise stop-drop-and-roll for real on a carpet after the sheet — the body remembers what the pencil rehearses. Never make fire scary-for-fun: firefighters are helpers, and practicing the move is what keeps children safe.

Understanding check: Ask: "What do firefighters spray from the hose? Show me stop-drop-and-roll. How many helmets?" Water, the move, the count = the sheet landed.

Real-life practice: Visit the drawing at bedtime: ask your child to SHOW the whole family how to stop, drop, and roll. Where is your family’s smoke alarm? Let your child find it — real maps of real safety.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: What a police officer carries and drives, which objects help keep people safe, and what a safe street crossing looks like.

Knowledge to have ready: Officers are neighborhood helpers we can trust: the badge shows who they are, the radio calls for help, the patrol car takes them quickly to where they are needed. In any real worry, the plan is the same — find a grown-up you know, and officers are helpers too.

Why this activity matters: Safety tools become recognizable when children sort them on paper. The crossing draw-prompt opens the family conversation about how WE cross — a conversation worth having a hundred times before it is ever needed.

  • Community helper vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Safety-object awareness
  • Counting to 5
  • Word tracing
  • Road-safety drawing

What to say before you start: "This is a police officer — a helper for the whole neighborhood. Trace the words, then connect the badge, the radio and the patrol car. Look at the six pictures: which ones help keep people safe? Count the cones carefully, then draw how WE cross the street safely."

What to look for on the sheet: Spot the gold badge on the cap and on the chest. In the grid, ask what each safety thing protects — a helmet protects heads, a cone warns cars, a first-aid kit helps hurts. In the draw box, ask for the stripes of the crosswalk before the pencil starts.

Questions to ask along the way: "What does the badge tell us?" "Which grid pictures keep people safe, and how?" "Who holds your hand when we cross?" "What do the cones tell cars to do?"

Helpful hints without giving it away: If the grid confuses, ask "does this protect a person or warn a car — or is it a toy?" The watch is the sneaky one: it tells time, but talk about whether it keeps someone SAFE. For the crossing drawing, stripes plus a grown-up’s hand are the key details.

Parent tips: Keep the message balanced — officers are helpers AND the first job in any worry is finding a grown-up you know. Practise the real crossing this week with the sheet’s words: stop, look, listen, hold hands.

Understanding check: Ask: "What does the radio do? Name two safety things from the grid. How do we cross the street?" Call-for-help, two objects, the family rule = the sheet landed.

Real-life practice: On the next walk, find one real safety thing from the grid — a cone, a helmet rider, a crossing — and name it on the spot. Real streets make the worksheet real.

Trace NURSE, match the nurse to the clipboard, bandage and thermometer, circle the healthy habits, count the bandages and draw one way a nurse helps people.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: Who nurses are and what they carry, which daily habits keep bodies healthy, and caring-in-action — the worksheet’s last box asks your child to draw a nurse’s kindness.

Knowledge to have ready: Nurses take care of people beside doctors: the clipboard keeps notes, the bandage protects a scrape, the thermometer checks temperature. Nurses explain every step and have gentle hands — a friendly face at any check-up.

Why this activity matters: Meeting the nurse on paper makes real check-ups calmer, and the healthy-habit grid doubles as the family’s daily-health talk. The big bandage count is honest two-row counting practice with a purpose.

  • Community helper vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Healthy habits
  • Counting to 10
  • Word tracing
  • Empathy drawing

What to say before you start: "This is a nurse — she takes care of people with gentle hands. Trace her name, then connect her to the clipboard, the bandage and the thermometer. Now the five pictures: which are healthy habits? Count every bandage slowly — there are two rows — and draw how a nurse helps."

What to look for on the sheet: Find the cross on the clipboard and the stethoscope around the nurse’s neck. In the grid, ask why each circled habit helps the body. In the count, touch each bandage left to right, top row first — two rows of five make ten.

Questions to ask along the way: "What does the thermometer check?" "Which habits did you circle, and when did you last do one?" "How many bandages in the top row? And the bottom?" "What would you want a nurse to say to you?"

Helpful hints without giving it away: The burger-and-fries tile is the trap — treats are fine sometimes, but ask "is this an every-day food or a sometimes food?" For the count, if ten wobbles, count the top row, tap your head, count the bottom row, then add the two numbers.

Parent tips: If a real check-up is coming, this sheet is the warm-up: the nurse will explain first, and telling her how you feel is always allowed. Praise gentle hands during the drawing — kindness is the lesson under the lesson.

Understanding check: Ask: "Who takes care of people beside the doctor? Name one healthy habit you circled. How many bandages?" The team, one habit, ten = the sheet landed.

Real-life practice: Play nurse with a teddy tonight: wrap a toilet-paper bandage, check temperature with a hand on the forehead, explain every step out loud — exactly the worksheet, warm and alive.

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: What a teacher’s day is full of — books, pencils, a board and questions — plus which objects help learning happen and how to write the word TEACHER.

Knowledge to have ready: Teachers help children learn letters, numbers, stories and how to be good friends. The board shows the lesson, the book holds the story, the pencil writes the practice. Your child already knows this world — the sheet names it.

Why this activity matters: A child who can name the teacher’s tools walks into any classroom feeling at home. The favorite-thing draw box turns the sheet into a small show-and-tell, and the pencil count is real counting with a real object.

  • School vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Learning-object awareness
  • Counting to 4
  • Word tracing
  • Self-expression drawing

What to say before you start: "This is a teacher — she helps children learn new things every day. Trace her name, then connect the book, the pencil and the board. Look at the five pictures: which help us learn? Count the pencils with your finger, and then draw the thing YOU love learning most."

What to look for on the sheet: Find the ABC-123 poster, the chalkboard and the pointer stick in the big picture. In the row, ask what each circled object does for learning. The apple sits with the school things for a reason — ask your child who traditionally gets an apple!

Questions to ask along the way: "What does the teacher write on the board?" "Which pictures help us learn — and what does each one do?" "How many pencils?" "What is YOUR favorite thing to learn, and who teaches it to you?"

Helpful hints without giving it away: The soccer ball is the playground guest — learning happens outside too, but the sheet asks for learning TOOLS. In the count, pencils lie at a slant; touch each tip so the count stays true.

Parent tips: Ask your child to teach the sheet back to you — playing teacher with the worksheet is the deepest rehearsal there is. Name real teachers your child knows and what each one is teaching them this year.

Understanding check: Ask: "What does a teacher do all day? Name three learning tools. How many pencils?" Helps-us-learn, three objects, four = the sheet landed.

Real-life practice: Tonight, your child plays teacher with teddies as the class: board, book, pencil — the whole lesson. Ten minutes of teaching-back beats an hour of being taught.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: Who librarians are and what a library holds — books, cards, shelves and computers — plus which everyday objects really belong there and how to write the word LIBRARIAN.

Knowledge to have ready: A librarian helps people find and borrow books: the library card takes books home for a while, the bookshelf keeps every story tidy, and each book comes back so a friend can enjoy it next. Libraries are quiet, friendly places full of stories.

Why this activity matters: A child who knows how the library works owns it for life. Naming the librarian’s tools turns a first visit from overwhelming to exciting, and the find-it-in-a-library grid builds the careful sorting that later sorts letters, numbers and bugs.

  • Community helper vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Place-based sorting
  • Word tracing
  • Counting practice
  • Favorite-book drawing

What to say before you start: "This is a librarian — she helps people find wonderful books. Trace her name, then connect the books, the library card and the bookshelf. Now look at the six pictures: which ones could you find in a library? Count the books slowly with your finger, and finish by drawing the book YOU love."

What to look for on the sheet: In the match row, ask which of the three things you hold, which you tuck in a pocket and which stands tall against the wall. In the grid, ask your child to tell a tiny story about each circled picture — librarians love stories. In the draw box, ask for the book’s title out loud before the pencil starts.

Questions to ask along the way: "What does a librarian do all day?" "Which grid pictures could you find at the library?" "What do we do with a book when we finish it?" "What is YOUR favorite book, and who reads it with you?"

Helpful hints without giving it away: Three tiles are worth a family debate: the apple and the scissors live in kitchens and desks, the globe might stand in a library corner, and one bouncy thing belongs on the grass — ask of each: "would I see this on my library visit?" For the count, touch each book spine once.

Parent tips: Pair the sheet with a real library trip this week — let your child carry the card and hand the books over the desk. Owning the borrowing-and-returning ritual is what quietly makes a reader.

Understanding check: Ask: "Who helps you find books? Name two things you saw at the library. How many books?" The helper, two finds, the count = the sheet landed.

Real-life practice: Visit the library and play find-it: the bookshelf, the computer, the desk — every circled picture spotted in real life. Then borrow one book and let your child check it out all by themselves.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: What a farmer grows and raises, which foods start on a farm, and how to tell farm things from store things — plus how to write the word FARMER.

Knowledge to have ready: Farmers grow food and care for animals: the tractor pulls and plows, the watering can gives thirsty plants a drink, and vegetables come out of the ground or off the plant. Apples grow on trees, cows give milk, and corn grows tall.

Why this activity matters: Knowing where food comes from is a superpower for picky eaters — a child who has circled the carrot on a farm sheet meets it on the plate with new interest. The farm grid also plants early thinking about how the world makes things.

  • Farm and food vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Where-food-comes-from sorting
  • Word tracing
  • Counting practice
  • Farm-scene drawing

What to say before you start: "This is a farmer — he grows food and takes care of animals. Trace his name, then connect the tractor, the watering can and the vegetables. Now look at the six pictures: which ones belong on a farm? Count the carrots and beets slowly, and then draw what YOU would see on a farm."

What to look for on the sheet: Find the vegetables in the match row and name each one. In the grid, ask where each food comes from — a tree, the ground, or a restaurant kitchen. In the count row, carrots and beets sit together, so touch each vegetable once and keep the running count out loud.

Questions to ask along the way: "What does a tractor do on a farm?" "Which foods in the grid grew on a farm?" "Have you ever pulled a carrot out of the ground?" "What would you feed a cow or a chicken?"

Helpful hints without giving it away: One tile in the grid comes hot from an oven nobody keeps on a farm — ask "did this grow anywhere, or did somebody bake it?" For the count, carrots and beets look different but both count: touch each vegetable once.

Parent tips: Next grocery trip, play farm-detective: find three foods from the grid and ask who grew each one. If your child is a picky eater, let THEM pick a vegetable from the count row at the store — ownership grows appetites.

Understanding check: Ask: "Who grows our food? Name two things that live or grow on a farm. Which food in the grid does NOT?" The farmer, two farm things, the baked one = the sheet landed.

Real-life practice: Try one farm food this week in its simplest form — corn on the cob, a raw carrot with its green top, an apple straight from the bag. Real food, real story, better eating.

FOR GROWN-UPS

What this worksheet teaches.

What the child is learning: What a chef does in a kitchen, which tools cook a meal, and which foods help bodies grow — plus how to write the short but mighty word CHEF.

Knowledge to have ready: A chef cooks for other people: the spoon stirs, the mixing bowl holds everything together, and the tall hat is called a toque — real chefs really wear it! Kitchens are busy places where good food and clean hands matter most.

Why this activity matters: Chefs make healthy food look exciting, and this sheet borrows that magic. The healthy-food grid turns into a plate conversation at exactly the age when food habits form, and the meal-drawing box lets your child design a menu of their own.

  • Kitchen vocabulary
  • Tool matching
  • Healthy-food sorting
  • Word tracing
  • Counting practice
  • Meal drawing

What to say before you start: "This is a chef — he cooks wonderful food for people. Trace his name, then connect the spoon, the mixing bowl and the hat. Now look at the six foods: which ones are healthy helpers for your body? Count the plates carefully, and then draw the meal YOU would love to make."

What to look for on the sheet: Find the chef’s tall hat and ask why chefs wear it. In the grid, sort the foods into every-day foods and sometimes foods out loud. In the draw box, ask for one vegetable on the plate before the pencil starts — real chefs put color on every plate.

Questions to ask along the way: "What does the chef stir in the big bowl?" "Which foods did you circle, and why?" "What is a sometimes food in our family?" "What would your restaurant serve first?"

Helpful hints without giving it away: Treats are allowed in life, but this grid asks for the foods that grow and give strength — ask of each: "every-day food or sometimes food?" For the count, plates can stack: count the rims, one touch each.

Parent tips: Let tonight’s dinner be the drawn meal for real if you can — even one food from your child’s menu on the plate makes the worksheet delicious. Chefs wash hands first: borrow that rule too.

What the child is learning: What a crossing guard does at the corner, the four rules of a safe street crossing, and which rules are safe and which are not — plus how to write the words CROSSING GUARD.

Knowledge to have ready: A crossing guard stops traffic so children can cross: the stop sign tells cars to wait, the bright vest makes the guard easy to see, and the crosswalk is the one place feet belong on the road. The rules: look left, right, then left again; raise your hand and wait; use the crosswalk — never run across.

Why this activity matters: Street crossing is the highest-stakes skill on the whole neighborhood walk, and rehearsal is what makes it stick. Sorting safe from unsafe rules lets your child explain the WHY back to you — a far stronger memory than a rule recited once.

What to look for on the sheet: Find the stripes on the crosswalk and the bright color of the vest. In the grid, read each rule aloud and ask your child to act the safe ones out and shout NO at the unsafe one — running across never wins. In the draw box, the left-right-left eyes are the detail that matters.

Questions to ask along the way: "What does the stop sign tell the cars?" "Which three rules are safe?" "Why do we look left, right, then left again?" "Who holds your hand at the crossing — and when may you cross alone?"

Helpful hints without giving it away: Three rules keep feet safe and one rule is a trick — the trick one is the fastest, and fast is exactly what roads do not like. Read every rule out loud before circling; the ears catch what the eyes skim.

Understanding check: Ask: "Who stops the cars at the corner? Name two safe crossing rules. Is running across safe or unsafe?" The guard, two rules, unsafe = the sheet landed.

Real-life practice: On every walk this week, let your child be the crossing captain: stop at the curb, look left-right-left, hold hands, walk. Ten real crossings beat ten worksheets — and you will both know the rules by heart.

Understanding check: Ask: "Who watches the pool? Name one safe rule and one unsafe rule you caught. What does the red cross mean?" The lifeguard, the rules, no-never = the sheet landed.

Real-life practice: At the next pool or bath, rehearse the sheet: grown-up first, walking feet, ask permission. Give your child the job of spotting the real lifeguard at every pool you visit — the watcher of the water, found in real life.

Now the six pictures: which ones really work in a lab? Let’s talk about each one. Count the test tubes in the rack, and then draw something YOU would love to discover."

What to look for on the sheet: Find the goggles and ask what they protect — a scientist’s eyes come first! In the grid, go tile by tile and ask where each thing really lives: the lab, the kitchen, the library or the craft drawer. In the count row, test tubes stand in a rack like crayons in a box — count left to right, one touch each.

Questions to ask along the way: "What does the microscope make bigger?" "Why does a scientist wear goggles?" "Which grid tiles belong to other rooms — and which rooms?" "What would YOU love to discover one day?"

Helpful hints without giving it away: Take each tile to its home: the lab, the fruit bowl, the bookshelf or the craft table — ask of each: would this sit on a lab bench, or somewhere else altogether? The goggles-and-gloves scientist only uses what belongs in the lab.

Parent tips: Labs have one big rule worth borrowing at home: real experiments happen WITH a grown-up and safety first. Do a kitchen-lab session — baking soda, vinegar, goggles from the dress-up box — and let your child narrate like the scientist they drew.

Understanding check: Ask: "Who asks questions for a living? Name two lab tools from the grid. What do the goggles protect?" The scientist, two tools, the eyes = the sheet landed.

Real-life practice: Do one tiny experiment this week — sink or float, baking-soda fizz, a magnifying glass over a leaf. Ask first, guess second, watch third: that order IS science, and your child just did it.
